relationship: Same-chapter distinct continuation list under the Jerusalem offspring notice
rationale: The separate unit preserves Samae, Iessibath, Nathan and its remaining supplied names after the preceding birth heading and shorter list; it is neither dropped nor collapsed into the earlier Nathan or assigned a newly reconciled total.

relationship: Foreign mobilisation after David's anointing with distinct narrated responses
rationale: Both say the foreigners seek David after hearing he was anointed king over Israel; Samuel says he went down to the stronghold while Chronicles says he went out to meet them, keeping both responses intact.

relationship: Same-chapter repeated Valley-of-the-Titans gathering
rationale: The first gathering in the Valley of the Titans is followed by another gathering there when the foreigners come again, identifying the repeated setting without resolving a modern site or importing a different valley title.

relationship: David's battle inquiry and explicit delivery answer repeated
rationale: Both quote David asking whether to advance and whether the foreigners will be delivered into his hands, followed by the Lord's Go up and delivery promise, rather than a reconstructed unrecorded oracle.

relationship: Victory described through the particular water-breakthrough metaphor
rationale: David attributes the enemy defeat to the Lord breaking through like waters; Chronicles likewise records a divine cutting-through like water. Upper Breaches and Cutting of Pharasin remain their supplied names without a new place-name equivalence claim.

relationship: Abandoned enemy gods with explicitly different handling notices
rationale: Both accounts report the foreigners abandoning their gods; Samuel says David and his men took them, whereas Chronicles adds an order to burn them, without inserting that order into Samuel's shorter statement.

relationship: Same-chapter renewed enemy gathering repeats the earlier valley setting
rationale: The foreigners come up again and gather in the same stated Valley of the Titans, recalling their first gathering without merging the two subsequent sets of divine directions.

relationship: Same-chapter distinct answers to the two battle inquiries
rationale: The later inquiry receives Do not go up to meet them and a turning movement near the place of weeping, contrasting the earlier Go up answer; the two particular commands are not silently made identical.

relationship: Sound-triggered advance and the Lord going before the army
rationale: Both accounts make a heard sound the condition for moving and say the Lord goes before to strike; the closing grove of weeping and shaking pear-tree tops remain distinct actual descriptions without a new botanical explanation.

relationship: Narrated obedience and the paired campaign endpoints
rationale: Both report carrying out God's command and striking the foreigners along named endpoints; Gibeon/Gezer and Gabaon/Gazara are preserved without claiming new linguistic or modern geographic verification.

relationship: Same-chapter seventy-thousand gathering introduces the ark ascent
rationale: David's gathering of about seventy thousand is followed by the movement to bring up God's ark, identifying the particular purpose while retaining the actual figure rather than replacing it with thirty thousand.

relationship: The ark and cherubim linked with the Lord's presence and speech
rationale: The procession description invokes the Lord's name and enthronement over the cherubim; Exodus specifies the ark cover and the Lord speaking from between its cherubim, providing the particular sacred-object background without reconstructing its current manufacture.

relationship: Same-chapter cart transport precedes the particular ark-gripping incident
rationale: The ark is placed on a new cart driven by Uzzah and his brothers; the later unit describes the calf pulling it aside and Uzzah gripping the ark, without supplying the absent name Ahio or resolving Abinadab against another book's household name.

relationship: Same-chapter walking brothers continue the stated cart scene
rationale: The continuation says his brothers walked before the ark after the new-cart notice identifies Uzzah and his brothers as Abinadab's sons; the supplied plural is kept rather than replaced with a newly named single driver.

relationship: Musical ark celebration with shared and distinct instruments
rationale: Both describe David and Israel celebrating before God with strength, lyres, harps, tambourines and cymbals; Samuel's pipes and Chronicles' trumpets remain different endings rather than an identical instrument inventory.

relationship: Touching the sacred object beside the explicit holy-object warning
rationale: Uzzah stretches out his hand and grips the ark after the calf pulls it aside; Numbers warns the sons of Kohath not to touch the holy things lest they die, supplying a particular legal comparison without inventing an additional charge in Samuel.

relationship: Same-chapter reported death follows the stated hand-to-ark act
rationale: The source reports God's anger, striking and Uzzah's death beside the ark after describing his grasp; it does not add an absent error formula or independently resolve the ultimate motive beyond the actual narration.

relationship: Same-chapter David's distress and breach-name notice follow Uzzah's death
rationale: David is disheartened because the Lord made a breach against Uzzah after the reported divine striking and death; Breach of Uzzah remains the supplied naming explanation without a new original-language etymology.

relationship: David's explicit fear and ark-arrival question in parallel accounts
rationale: Both say David feared God that day and asked how God's ark could come to him, a particular shared question without equating every differently named participant in the surrounding narratives.

relationship: Same-chapter diversion to Obed-edom followed by the stated residence
rationale: David declines to bring the ark into his city and diverts it to Obed-edom's house; the next unit places its three-month stay there, without changing the host's supplied Gittite designation.

relationship: Same-chapter household blessing becomes the explicit report to David
rationale: The narrator states Obed-edom's household was blessed during the ark's stay; David is then told of that blessing because of the ark, connecting the particular event and report without inferring every mechanism of blessing.

relationship: Same-chapter renewed transport responds to the preceding household blessing
rationale: David hears the blessing report and brings the ark from Obed-edom's house with gladness after the stated three-month residence, without treating every earlier transport detail as unchanged.

relationship: Ark-carrying sacrifices compared with distinct counts and animals
rationale: Samuel has seven dancing companies with a calf and a lamb; Chronicles has strengthened Levites carrying the ark and seven calves and seven rams. The procession-and-sacrifice connection preserves those different actors, counts and kinds.

relationship: David's processional robe in two specifically worded descriptions
rationale: Samuel clothes David in a distinctive robe while he plays on tuned instruments; Chronicles describes a fine-linen robe, without adding linen or an ephoud to Samuel's actual statement.

relationship: All-Israel ark ascent accompanied by explicit sounding instruments
rationale: Both describe all Israel bringing up the ark with sounding signals and trumpet language; the fuller Chronicles list is not imported into every word of Samuel's shorter shouting-and-trumpet notice.

relationship: Same-chapter Michal's heart response and later exposure remark
rationale: Michal despises David in her heart after seeing his dancing and playing; her later encounter is called a blessing and contains the public-uncovering remark, preserving both actual descriptions rather than rewriting either as an unreported curse.

relationship: Ark placed in David's tent with the stated offerings
rationale: Both place God's ark in the tent David pitched and name whole burnt offerings; Samuel's peace offerings and Chronicles' offerings of deliverance remain their supplied wording rather than a new ritual reconstruction.

relationship: Completed offerings followed by David blessing the people
rationale: Both explicitly report David finishing the offerings and then blessing the people in the Lord's name, without turning that sequence into proof of every later royal act's approval.

relationship: Bread distribution explicitly includes both men and women
rationale: Both accounts distribute bread portions to Israelites, men and women alike; Samuel's loaf, hearth cake and frying-pan flat cake are not replaced with Chronicles' baker's loaf and cake or an unprovided meat portion.

relationship: Same-chapter Michal's public-uncovering remark and David's particular reply
rationale: Michal's speech describes David's display before servant women; he answers with the Lord's choice above her father's house and his intention to dance, preserving the preceding blessed-him wording and the actual subjects of honour and worthlessness.

relationship: David's claimed choice above Saul beside the Jesse-house commission
rationale: David invokes the Lord choosing him above Michal's father and house; the earlier commission sends Samuel to Jesse after rejecting Saul's reign, without turning David's speech into independent approval of every part of the dispute.

relationship: Same-chapter servant-women language repeated in David's response
rationale: David's reply repeats the servant women named in Michal's exposure speech and speaks of being worthless in her eyes; the actual honour wording is kept without importing a different humility formulation.

relationship: Same-chapter childlessness notice closes the account of Michal's reaction
rationale: The closing notice says Michal had no child until her death after the account of her inward response; it states no medical diagnosis or express causal punishment, and this connection does not invent either.

relationship: Settled royal house after the reported cedar building
rationale: The oracle setting has the king settled in his house; the earlier narrative describes Tyre's builders making David a house and his understanding of the Lord's establishment, without dating every enemy's defeat independently.

relationship: David's cedar-house contrast with the ark's dwelling
rationale: Both accounts have David tell Nathan that he lives in a cedar house while the ark has a temporary dwelling; Samuel's tent and Chronicles' skins remain their actual descriptions.

relationship: Same-chapter Nathan's initial encouragement followed by the night prohibition
rationale: Nathan first encourages David because the Lord is with him; the night's divine word then says David will not build the house, distinguishing the initial counsel from the subsequent explicit message.

relationship: Nighttime divine-word introduction addressed to Nathan
rationale: Both introduce a word of the Lord to Nathan that night, tying the subsequent message to that particular named recipient without claiming a new unreported oracle.

relationship: Explicit prohibition on David building the divine dwelling
rationale: Both tell Nathan to address David as the Lord's servant and say he shall not build the house for God's dwelling, preserving the actual declarative prohibition rather than replacing it with a differently worded question.

relationship: Divine movement in tent and lodging since Israel's departure
rationale: Both contrast a permanent house with movement in tent and lodging since Israel was brought out; Samuel explicitly names Egypt, without requiring every word of the two notices to be identical.

relationship: The cedar-house question about Israel's appointed shepherd tribes
rationale: Both ask whether God ever demanded a cedar house from an appointed tribe shepherding Israel, preserving the actual tribes wording rather than substituting a separately inferred list of judges.

relationship: David's sheepfold-to-ruler commission repeated
rationale: Both say the Lord took David from the sheepfold to lead Israel; Chronicles adds following the flocks, without importing a different office or a new shepherding chronology.

relationship: Shepherd origin beside the actual youngest-son anointing
rationale: The divine speech recalls taking David from the sheepfold for rule; the earlier Jesse scene places the youngest with the flock before the Lord names David and Samuel anoints him, preserving the distinct recalled commission and narrated selection.

relationship: Presence, enemy destruction and a great name explicitly repeated
rationale: Both divine speeches recall being with David wherever he went, destroying enemies and making his name like the great ones, rather than identifying every enemy or claiming an exhaustive campaign catalogue.

relationship: Israel's planted place and relief from oppressive anxiety
rationale: Both promise a place to plant Israel, dwelling without anxiety and no renewed humbling as at the beginning, preserving the particular promised conditions rather than claiming their permanent historical completion.

relationship: Judges-and-enemies parallel with expressly different builder wording
rationale: Both recall appointed judges, enemies and a house announcement; Samuel says you will build Him a house, while Chronicles says the Lord will build you a house. This comparison retains the direction difference rather than harmonizing it.

relationship: Body-descended successor and prepared kingdom after David's death
rationale: Both promise offspring from David's body after his days and sleep with the fathers, with a prepared kingdom; the particular successor promise is not expanded into an unprovided succession date.

relationship: Davidic offspring and enduring throne promise in the covenant psalm
rationale: The speech promises David's bodily offspring a prepared kingdom; Psalm 88 explicitly names the covenant with David and preparing his seed for ever and his throne through generations, preserving the source edition's psalm numbering.

relationship: Successor building God's house and the forever throne
rationale: Both say the successor will build God a house and have his throne set upright for ever; Samuel additionally names My name, without supplying every later building detail.

relationship: The father-and-son formula explicitly reused concerning the Son
rationale: Samuel states I will be a father to him and he a son to Me; Hebrews repeats that formula in its discussion of the Son and angels. Hebrews does not quote Samuel's following wrongdoing-and-correction clause, which is not assigned to the Son by this comparison.

relationship: Conditional descendants' discipline with rod language and retained mercy
rationale: Samuel joins possible wrongdoing to correction with a human rod and afflictions; the psalm addresses sons abandoning the law, a rod and scourges, followed by mercy not withdrawn, preserving different formulations and recipients.

relationship: Mercy not withdrawn in the royal-son promise
rationale: Both divine speeches explicitly promise not to withdraw mercy as in the contrasting earlier case; Samuel's those removed before Me and Chronicles' those before you are retained without supplying an absent personal name.

relationship: Enduring mercy and covenant fidelity expressed beside royal discipline
rationale: Samuel promises not to withdraw mercy from the royal successor; the psalm says mercy will not be scattered away and the covenant will not be profaned, without declaring that no discipline can occur.

relationship: The enduring offspring-and-throne promise in royal speech and psalm
rationale: Samuel promises his house, kingdom and throne secure for ever before Me; the psalm promises his seed and throne enduring like sun and moon, preserving the supplied pronouns rather than replacing them with your house or before you.

relationship: Forever royal establishment with distinct house and pronoun wording
rationale: Samuel says his house and kingdom will be secure before Me; Chronicles says him secure in My house and in his kingdom. The shared enduring-throne promise is retained without silently making the house clauses identical.

relationship: Nathan's delivery explicitly follows the complete words and vision
rationale: Both narrator notices say Nathan spoke to David according to all these words and this vision, identifying the delivered message rather than claiming to recover further unsupplied material.

relationship: David's seated prayer opens with the who-am-I and house question
rationale: Both place David seated before the Lord and asking Who am I and what is my house; Samuel's loved me to this extent and Chronicles' loved me for ever remain distinct endings.

relationship: Future household speech beside differently stated human language
rationale: Both prayers call the preceding favour small and mention the servant's house far ahead; Samuel's law of the human being and Chronicles' human vision and exaltation are preserved without a new resolution of their differing clauses.

relationship: David's what-more question and God's knowledge of the servant
rationale: Both ask what more David can say or add and affirm that God knows His servant; the comparison keeps Chronicles' giving-glory wording without adding it to Samuel.

relationship: Greatness done according to the divine heart
rationale: Both prayers attribute the accomplished greatness to God's heart; Samuel further names His word and making it known to the servant, without presenting the shorter Chronicles unit as a full identical quotation.

relationship: None like God and the shared heard-with-ears confession
rationale: Both prayers say there is none like God and no other besides Him according to what was heard with the ears, preserving the actual confession rather than reconstructing an unreported earlier hearing.

relationship: Israel's Egyptian redemption and the divine-name language
rationale: Both prayers distinguish Israel through God's redemption from Egypt, making a name and driving out nations; Samuel's separate greatness, manifestation and dwellings wording is retained rather than silently merged into Chronicles' great-and-manifest-name formulation.

relationship: Israel prepared as God's enduring people and the mutual God relation
rationale: Both affirm Israel as God's people for ever and the Lord as their God, connecting those explicit paired covenant statements without an independently expanded membership definition.

relationship: Prayer that the spoken word concerning the servant's house stand for ever
rationale: Both prayers ask confirmation of God's word about the servant and his house, distinguishing the petition from a report that every later event has already fulfilled it.

relationship: Same-chapter repeated request for divine magnification
rationale: The short petition that God's name be magnified for ever returns to the earlier prayer that He may be magnified because there is none like Him; the particular magnification clauses are compared without adding a longer parallel unit to the source.

relationship: Revealed house promise expressly grounds the servant's prayer
rationale: Both prayers connect the opened or revealed ear concerning a house with finding heart or courage to pray; Samuel's explicit I will build you a house remains intact beside the earlier differently directed 7:11 clause.

relationship: God's identity and the good words concerning the servant
rationale: Both affirm Thou art God and the good things spoken concerning the servant; Samuel further declares His words true, without erasing that additional clause in a general paraphrase.

relationship: Household blessing requested or begun with an enduring horizon
rationale: Samuel asks God to begin and bless the servant's house for ever; Chronicles says He has begun and blessed, retaining the different petition and accomplished wording rather than making their tenses identical.
